candidates.attacker_control: Full content of the XML document handed to `XStream.fromXML(...)`/`unmarshal(...)`: element names/aliases, `class` and `resolves-to` attributes, nested objects, collection entries and serialized-data emulation nodes. The application only has to expose an endpoint that deserializes untrusted XML through a default-configured XStream instance.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The denials that do exist are enforced correctly: `NoPermission.allows` throws `ForbiddenClassException` rather than returning false (security/NoPermission.java:33-38), so the EventHandler block is effective and the classic DynamicProxy+EventHandler+ProcessBuilder chain is blocked; `CachingMapper` caches denials by name and cannot re-allow a denied name; XXE is separately mitigated (`disallow-doctype-decl` in DomDriver/Dom4JDriver/JDom*; `IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false` in Stax/Sjsxp/Wstx); CVE-2017-7957 void-type DoS is mitigated in BeanProvider/PureJavaReflectionProvider/SunLimitedUnsafeReflectionProvider; `SecurityMapper` is inside the mapper chain used by converters, and `resolves-to`/`class`/interface/`readResolve` names all pass through `mapper.realClass`. The residual issue is breadth of the denylist, not a broken check. The XStream docs themselves state a blacklist gives a 'false sense of security' and that the whitelist helper is opt-in, which supports (rather than refutes) the finding.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution / arbitrary command execution in the JVM processing the XML, with the application's privileges; additionally server-side request forgery, local file deletion and denial of service through the same arbitrary-instantiation primitive. This is the vulnerability class of CVE-2020-26217 (fixed in XStream 1.4.14).
candidates.prerequisites: Application (a) builds XStream without an explicit whitelist (`new XStream()` or a variant that leaves `setupSecurity()`'s defaults in place) and (b) unmarshals XML from an untrusted source. If the application calls `XStream.setupDefaultSecurity()` or establishes its own `allowTypes*` whitelist, the permissive ANY permission is cleared and the attack surface shrinks. A usable gadget/trigger class must be present on the classpath (the JDK itself provides many candidates when ANY is granted).
candidates.root_cause: `XStream.setupSecurity()` (XStream.java:639-649) initializes the default security framework with `AnyTypePermission.ANY` and only three denials: `java.beans.EventHandler`, `.*\$LazyIterator`, `javax.crypto..*`. `SecurityMapper.realClass()` (mapper/SecurityMapper.java:70-78) is the single authorization gate for every type resolved from the stream, so any other class on the classpath is accepted. The engine then instantiates the attacker-named class through `AbstractReflectionConverter.instantiateNewInstance` (AbstractReflectionConverter.java:569-582) and `PureJavaReflectionProvider.newInstance` (65-102, which force-accesses and invokes no-arg constructors), can build `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` instances from attacker-supplied interface lists and handler classes (DynamicProxyConverter.java:94-128), invokes attacker-controlled comparator/key methods while populating sorted collections (TreeMapConverter.java:103-132, TreeSetConverter.java:56-95) and emulates Java serialization by invoking readObject/readResolve on attacker-selected Serializable classes (SerializableConverter.java:312 ff.). A name denylist covering only EventHandler/lazy iterators/javax.crypto cannot cover the gadget space (e.g., `java.lang.ProcessBuilder` and its inner classes, other JDK InvocationHandler/trigger classes are not denied), which is exactly the insufficient-denylist problem fixed in 1.4.14.
candidates.title: Default XStream security setup allows arbitrary class instantiation from untrusted XML (incomplete default denylist -> RCE; CVE-2020-26217 class of issue)
candidates.trace: fromXML -> TreeUnmarshaller.start (TreeUnmarshaller.java:131-140) -> HierarchicalStreams.readClassType -> CachingMapper/AnnotationMapper -> SecurityMapper.realClass: only the three default denials throw `ForbiddenClassException`; all other classes pass because ANY is in the permission list (XStream.java:644). The selected converter then materializes the attacker-chosen type: AbstractReflectionConverter.instantiateNewInstance -> reflectionProvider.newInstance (arbitrary no-arg constructor invocation), DynamicProxyConverter creates a Proxy with attacker-chosen interfaces/handler, TreeMap/TreeSet/Collection converters invoke comparator or key `hashCode`/`compareTo` while inserting entries, and SerializableConverter/ExternalizableConverter invoke readObject/readResolve/readExternal. Any of these trigger primitives reaching a gadget class whose effect is `java.lang.ProcessBuilder.start()` (ProcessBuilder is not on the deny list) yields command execution; simpler gadgets yield SSRF, file deletion or DoS.
candidates.unverified: The exact end-to-end gadget chain and required classpath classes were not established (no execution/scanner run, no tests in the snapshot); I could not read the 1.4.14 fix commit or its regression-test payload, so the precise deny-list entries the maintainers considered missing are unconfirmed. Runtime exploitability therefore remains a lead, not a confirmed result.

coverage_summary: 484 model-visible files (416 Java; remainder POMs/HTML/XML docs). The snapshot contains no unit-test sources, so only main code and distribution/benchmark modules were reviewable. I read the full security framework (SecurityMapper, all TypePermission classes, NoPermission), the mapper chain construction and CachingMapper, the core unmarshalling path (TreeUnmarshaller, AbstractReflectionConverter, SerializableConverter, ExternalizableConverter, DynamicProxyConverter, TreeMap/TreeSet/Collection converters, PureJavaReflectionProvider), XML drivers' XXE hardening, the persistence module, XStreamer and the XStream facade, plus the project security/CVE documentation. P1 index: 416 parsed Java files, 4 omitted files, 1 parse error, syntax-only relations with no control-flow/data-flow; every indexed lead I used was re-verified against source text. Not exhaustively line-reviewed: xstream-jmh/xstream-benchmark modules, most io/xml driver internals, several extended/basic converters, and the xstream-hibernate module (spot-checked only).
limitations: No tests are present in the snapshot, so the upstream security regression test/payload for the 1.4.14 fix could not be inspected.
No code was executed and no exploit was attempted; all conclusions are static source reading, so the finding is a lead rather than a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

The P1 relation index is syntactic only (no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, runtime reachability, or DI/security enforcement), and it reported 4 omitted files and 1 parse error; findings were verified manually in source instead.
I could not consult the fixed version or CVE patch (external access prohibited), so the exact missing deny-list entries in 1.4.14 are inferred from version/context and source state, not verified.
Coverage is strongest in the security and unmarshalling paths; other modules (jmh/benchmark, hibernate, some converters/drivers) were only spot-checked.

rejected_leads.reason: The repository FAQ still lists these two drivers as vulnerable because their parser cannot disable parameter entities, but the main drivers explicitly disable DOCTYPE/external entities and using those drivers is an explicit application choice; this is a documented limitation rather than the snapshot's next-fix security defect.

rejected_leads.lead: XStreamer.fromXML deserializes an embedded XStream instance via Java serialization
rejected_leads.reason: It applies `XStream.setupDefaultSecurity` to the outer stream and the embedded-configuration behavior is the documented purpose of the API; exploitation requires the application to route untrusted XML into this specialized helper, and the type whitelist for the outer stream exists. No concrete bypass was traced in source.

Filenames are built by escaping the key's type/value with '/' '\' and '%' in the illegal-character set, so no traversal was demonstrated; `unescape` assumes well-formed `%XX` input but only sees names produced by `escape`.

This is the documented Java-serialization integration API; the library warns it is unsafe for untrusted data. The XStream XML path itself passes object types through SecurityMapper, so this alone is not the snapshot's strongest defect.
Already mitigated in this snapshot through explicit void/Void rejection in BeanProvider, PureJavaReflectionProvider and SunLimitedUnsafeReflectionProvider, and PrimitiveTypePermission.

summary: XStream 1.4.14-SNAPSHOT (post-1.4.13) with the default security framework. The strongest issue is the insecure-by-default type denylist used during XML unmarshalling: a plain `new XStream()` grants `AnyTypePermission.ANY` and denies only `java.beans.EventHandler`, `.*\$LazyIterator` and `javax.crypto.*`, while the unmarshalling engine reflectively instantiates arbitrary classes, builds attacker-specified dynamic proxies, invokes comparator/hashCode methods while populating collections, and emulates readObject/readResolve for Serializable types. This is the blacklist-bypass class of issue addressed by XStream 1.4.14 (CVE-2020-26217) and, per the project's own docs, provides only a "false sense of security"; the only robust mitigation (`XStream.setupDefaultSecurity(xstream)` whitelist) is opt-in. I found no stronger, better-evidenced issue.
